issues.legal_issue: A statutory tribunal cannot substantively review an earlier order unless legislation specifically confers that power.
material_facts: A Competent Officer had ordered the disputed property transferred to the respondent on payment of an assessed amount.
The appellant, which had not been a party to the original proceedings, later applied to the Competent Officer for review and transfer of the property to itself.
The Competent Officer reviewed the earlier order, held it illegal, and directed that the property be sold in the open market; the Appellate Officer confirmed that order.

The Act provided for appeals and revision and allowed correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors arising from accidental slips or omissions, but the Court found no provision conferring the substantive review power exercised.
issues.conclusion: The Competent Officer lacked power to review the earlier order in the manner undertaken, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A tribunal has no inherent power to review its earlier order; that power must be specifically conferred by statute. Section 16 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 permitted correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors caused by accidental slips or omissions, not substantive review. Sections 14 and 15 dealt with appeals and revision. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.challenge_to_tribunal_review_order: A party appealed against an order made by a statutory tribunal after it reconsidered an earlier order.
predicates.review_authority_not_conferred: The governing law did not confer on the tribunal authority to substantively review the earlier order.
predicates.correction_power_is_limited_to_accidenta: The tribunal's relevant correction authority was confined to clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors arising from accidental slips or omissions.
predicates.substantive_review_power_absent: The tribunal had no authority to make the substantive review order.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a tribunal's reconsideration of an earlier order, and the law does not confer substantive review authority or permits only correction of accidental errors, the tribunal lacks substantive review power.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider contentions that were not raised before the court below or included in the relevant applications for leave to appeal.
material_facts: The appellant sought to raise several contentions before the Supreme Court.
Those contentions had not been raised before the High Court Division Bench and were not included in the petition for special leave or the petition seeking leave to appeal from the High Court.
The Supreme Court declined to allow the appellant to agitate those contentions.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not permit the appellant to raise the new contentions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court confined consideration to the issue that had been presented before the High Court Division Bench and reflected in the applications for leave to appeal; it did not consider the newly raised contentions.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party presented contentions in an appeal to a higher court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_below: The party had not raised the contention before the relevant court below.
predicates.contention_omitted_from_leave_applicatio: The party had not included the contention in the applications seeking leave to appeal.
predicates.new_contention_not_considered: The higher court declined to consider the new contention.

issues.definition: In an appellate proceeding, a contention not raised below and omitted from the applications for leave to appeal is not considered.
